The Common firecrest (Regulus ignicapillus) is a small insectivorous passerine that exhibits a rapid developmental trajectory. Eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] typically complete their development in about 15.5 days [ab = about 15.5 days], a value consistent with the short incubation periods observed across the Regulidae. At hatching, altricial nestlings emerge with a wet weight at birth of merely 0.76 grams [Wwb = 0.76 grams], reflecting the extremely limited yolk reserves typical of passerine hatchlings. This initial mass stands in stark contrast to the ultimate wet weight of approximately 10 grams [Wwi = approximately 10 grams] attained by fledglings, representing more than a thirteen-fold increase over the roughly two-week nestling period. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of active metabolic output in this species, measured at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the nest-dwelling young achieve fledging status after 16.5 days [tx = 16.5 days] following hatching, after which they remain dependent on parental provisioning for a further period.

This relatively early onset of gonadal maturation is unusual among small temperate passerines and may relate to their high metabolic rate. Following the attainment of sexual maturity, a substantial period of somatic growth and behavioral maturation elapses before the first successful breeding attempt. With regard to annual productivity, the Common firecrest displays a notable capacity for multiple broods within a single breeding season, a life-history strategy that compensates for its relatively small clutch size. Females produce clutches containing up to 11 eggs [N_R_i = clutches containing up to 11 eggs], though more typically 7 to 9 eggs are laid. Second broods are common, contributing to a maximum reproductive rate achieved through approximately 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches per year], yielding a maximum annual output of up to 22 eggs per year [Ri = up to 22 eggs per year]. These measurements were recorded during periods when the birds are maintaining standard active body temperatures of 41.6 °C, representing optimal thermal conditions for sustained metabolic output. The combination of a relatively high per-clutch fecundity and the ability to rear two successful broods positions the species as a comparatively productive member of the sylviid warblers, offsetting the high juvenile mortality inherent in its altricial developmental mode.

Comparative longevity data for the Common firecrest remain somewhat limited, but life-history tables constructed from congeneric information, specifically that of the goldcrest (Regulus regulus) as cataloged in the AnAge database, provide a useful benchmark. Based on this comparative framework, the maximum lifespan in the wild is estimated at approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years], a value that was recorded under the typical active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This longevity figure suggests a relatively high annual adult survival rate for a bird of such diminutive size, which is exceptional given its high metabolic costs. Attaining an age of 7 years is likely contingent upon surviving the perilous first winter, a major selective bottleneck for juvenile firecrests. Adult survival benefits from their largely insectivorous diet, which provides adequate nutrition during the breeding season, although winter months impose significant energetic challenges that limit the realized lifespan for most individuals in the population.
